documents.abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is \textbf{per-instruction credit attribution} and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose \textbf{EDIC}, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7\% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5\% on Qwen3-4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.

Background: Examination periods require students to maintain prolonged static postures while sitting, reading, and writing continuously for extended durations.Such postural demands, combined with limited movement opportunities, may contribute to musculoskeletal discomfort and pain.However, limited evidence is available regarding the immediate musculoskeletal effects of examination-related static posture among college students.Objective: To investigate the immediate effect of examination-related static posture on the musculoskeletal system and to identify the prevalence and characteristics of post-examination musculoskeletal discomfort among college students.Methodology: An observational cross-sectional survey study was conducted among 350 college students aged 17-45 years who appeared for written examinations lasting at least one hour.Data were collected immediately after examinations using a self-structured questionnaire.Information regarding demographic characteristics, postural habits, ergonomic factors, examination-related stress, uniform-related discomfort, and musculoskeletal symptoms was obtained.Pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS).Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and presented as frequencies and percentages.Results: Among the participants, 88.6% reported sitting continuously for at least one hour during examinations, 80.9% leaned forward while writing, and 65.1% maintained prolonged neck flexion.Examination-related stress was reported by 80% of students.Immediate post-examination musculoskeletal pain was reported by 65.1% of participants.Pain most commonly developed after the examination (52.9%) and was predominantly intermittent in nature (74.6%).Pain disturbed concentration in 66.0% of participants and affected sleep in 57.4%.Although 82.3% reported symptom relief after rest, 54.0% stated that discomfort persisted even after reaching home.Additional observations indicated recurrent musculoskeletal symptoms among students who completed the questionnaire following multiple examination sessions.Conclusion: Examination-related static posture is associated with a high prevalence of immediate musculoskeletal discomfort among college students.Prolonged continuous sitting, forward leaning posture while writing, sustained neck flexion, and examination-related stress emerged as the major contributing factors associated with post-examination musculoskeletal pain.The findings emphasize the importance of ergonomic awareness, proper sitting posture, regular postural adjustments, and appropriate examination seating arrangements to reduce musculoskeletal discomfort and promote students' well-being and academic performance.

Heterogeneous unmanned vehicles system, comprising Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs), offer complementary advantages in Search and Rescue missions. However, the impact of different vehicle combinations on operator remains unclear. This study investigated how unmanned vehicle combinations (1UAV+3UGV, 2UAV+2UGV, and 3UAV+1UGV) influence operator performance and workload in Search and Rescue scenario. Thirty-six participants performed the simulated missions. The results indicate that the balanced 2UAV+2UGV combination leads to higher performance and lower workload. To identify underlying mechanisms, participants were grouped by median performance and workload. High-performance participants exhibited a more proactive and efficient information acquisition strategy, flexibly allocating attention through more frequent saccades and fixation transitions between critical areas. Additionally, higher perceived workload was associated with a video-centric attention pattern that may reflect visual tunneling and limit the acquisition of global mission information. This research integrates vehicle combination and cognitive mechanisms to inform the design of heterogeneous unmanned systems.

The impact of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazards on the Quality of Work Life (QWL) of the employees of the food industry in Pakistan has been studied. Food manufacturing operations are often dangerous, and workers are likely to be exposed to physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychological, mechanical and electrical hazards. A quantitative research method was followed with a cross-sectional survey design, and 121 total employees of food processing organisations of Pakistan participated in the study to collect data across the various departments of these food processing organisations. The relationships between OHS hazards and QWL were analyzed by using SPSS using correlation and multiple regression analyses. The results indicate that the chemical and ergonomic hazards are the most important factors influencing QWL, followed by psychological hazards, physical hazards, mechanical hazards and electrical hazards, with biological hazards not being statistically significant. The findings reflect the multi-faceted impact of work safety on employees' wellbeing, satisfaction, and work-life balance. This study adds to the very few studies conducted on the OHS of food industry workers in Pakistan and offers implications for improving worksite safety, optimizing worker health, and improving organizational productivity.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In team sports, psychological regulation is crucial, yet traditional methods lack personalization, rely on subjective assessments, and offer low realism. This study examined the integration of computer-assisted technologies into psychological training. A six-month trial involved 90 professional football, basketball, and ice hockey players, randomly assigned to an experimental group or control group. Data on physiology, psychology, performance, and team communication were analyzed using t-tests. Per the results, the experimental group showed 21.3% lower anxiety, 25.4% higher cohesion, 21.2% faster decision response, 14.3% higher clutch success, 38.7% better communication efficiency; clutch error rate was also reduced from 27% to 11%. However, ~15% experienced virtual reality discomfort, and artificial intelligence overreliance reduced tactical creativity by 19%. Computer-assisted technologies enhance psychological resilience and team performance. Balancing data-driven precision with human-centered coaching is vital. Future work should optimize training models and establish data ethics.

Abstract Background Postpolypectomy surveillance intervals derived from colonoscopy findings and histopathology should be guideline-based, yet these are frequently not adhered to, contributing to under- and oversurveillance. This motivates a more structured and automated approach to improve adherence. Objective We developed and evaluated an automated, implementable, guideline-aligned decision support tool that extracts colorectal polyp features from free-text colonoscopy and histopathology reports and produces auditable surveillance recommendations. Methods We extracted paired colonoscopy and histopathology reports from a National Health Service (NHS) trust and designed a 4-stage prompting pipeline using open-weight large language models to separate multispecimen histopathology reports into individual containers (“pots”), align endoscopic findings with specimens, and normalize each pot into a structured schema. The surveillance intervals were then computed by a deterministic rule engine encoding guideline rules. We evaluated extraction performance on 100 procedures (215 pots), assessed surveillance recommendation performance on a same-site cohort (n=100), and performed external validation on a cohort from a second trust (n=100). A separate retrospective audit compared automated recommendations and observed routine scheduling against a clinician-derived reference based on full electronic health record review in 127 patients. Results Key extraction fields showed end-to-end accuracy (specimen type=0.995; location=0.981; diagnosis=0.981; excision completeness=0.949), with mean report-level pot comprehensiveness of 0.968 (SD 0.112). Overall surveillance recommendation accuracy was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98) at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT) and 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) at Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust (SWB) and showed strong class-level performance ( no follow-up F 1 -score of 0.98 at GSTT and 0.97 at SWB; site check F 1 -score of 0.93 at GSTT and 0.91 at SWB; 3-year follow-up F 1 -score of 0.86 at GSTT and 0.80 at SWB; cancer alert F 1 -score of 1.00 at GSTT and 1.00 at SWB). The comparison to current clinical practice showed that the tool would improve guideline adherence primarily by reducing potential undersurveillance. Conclusions This hybrid approach using open-weight large language models for structured extraction and guideline-encoded rules for decision-making can generate accurate, lightweight, and auditable postpolypectomy surveillance recommendations. Such a tool has the potential to improve safety netting and guideline adherence in NHS colonoscopy workflows.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Intelligence Seed 001 project is a protocol-neutral, machine-readable research prompt exploring how life creates opportunities for new forms of information processing, how cognition is externalized through technology, and how human and artificial intelligence depend on resilient civilization-scale infrastructure.

Sepsis is a major public health concern, and many sepsis patients die due to ineffective hemodynamic management. Artificial intelligence could support hemodynamic decisions, particularly in complex cases where conflicting information and comorbidities drive uncertainty and practice variation. However, these systems' real-world value depends on not just accuracy, but how they influence the quality of clinician decisions. We first retrospectively evaluated an AI system's recommendations in 6,928 sepsis patients, finding that they improved upon the original providers' decisions overall but had significantly worse performance in complex cases. We then conducted a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians to test their use of this imperfect advice in six complex treatment decisions, using one of three advice types designed to vary reasoning autonomy. Participants given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, choosing optimal treatments in 56.3% of decisions compared to 31.8% if they had always followed the recommendations. They also made significantly better decisions than those receiving a less prescriptive advice type (42.9%). Physicians selectively adapted and improved weak advice, likely because it prompted them to reconsider their assessment. Our findings suggest that improving sepsis care decisions with AI may require accounting for these indirect influences resulting from human-AI collaborative reasoning.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in physical products, from domestic appliances and vehicles to medical devices and wearables, yet the success of such products depends less on algorithmic performance than on whether people understand, trust and meaningfully integrate them into everyday life. This paper examines the contribution of industrial product design to the current need for, and use of, AI. Through a conceptual and integrative narrative review of literature in design research, human–computer interaction (HCI), computational design and AI ethics, it develops an analytical framework of five contributions: (1) framing human needs so that AI addresses problems worth solving; (2) making AI capabilities legible through form, interaction and feedback; (3) calibrating trust and control; (4) embedding AI in sustainable and ethical product lifecycles; and (5) integrating AI as a tool within the design process itself. The analysis indicates that industrial design acts as a mediating layer between technological capability and human practice, and that its contribution lies as much in deciding where AI should not be used as in enabling it. The paper closes with implications for practice, education and policy, and five propositions for empirical testing.

Brands are increasingly partnering with AI-generated influencers — computer-generated personas that post, endorse, and interact on social media. Whether such endorsers can build the credibility on which purchase decisions depend remains unclear. This study examines the effect of five attributes of AI-generated influencers — Perceived Realism, Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Expertise, Parasocial Interaction, and Perceived Transparency (AI disclosure) — on Brand Credibility, and tests the role of Brand Credibility in shaping Purchase Intention.A descriptive and analytical research design was adopted, and primary data were collected from 400 social media users in Tamil Nadu who had encountered branded content from AI-generated influencers, using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and stratified random sampling by age group. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and bootstrapped mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4).All five attributes significantly predicted Brand Credibility, with Perceived Authenticity (β = 0.268) and Perceived Expertise (β = 0.206) strongest; the model explained 59.0% of its variance. Brand Credibility strongly predicted Purchase Intention (β = 0.424), and the full model explained 64.2% of the variance in intention. Brand Credibility significantly mediated all five relationships, fully for Perceived Realism and Perceived Transparency and partially for the others. The findings offer implications for brands, agencies, and regulators on the use and disclosure of AI-generated influencers
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: This article critically evaluates eight emerging directions in social media marketing for tourism and examines whether their growing practical adoption is supported by peer-reviewed empirical evidence. Particular attention is paid to the attribution gap between platform-level exposure and engagement metrics and subsequent tourism outcomes, including destination consideration, bookings, tourist expenditure, and post-visit advocacy. The study employs a structured literature review and conceptual analysis. Peer-reviewed research in tourism and hospitality, including recent systematic reviews, constitutes the primary evidence base. Official statistics, platform-reported data, and industry statistics are used exclusively to provide contextual information and are assessed according to the transparency of their sources. Assessments of adoption levels and evidence strength are explicitly analytical judgments rather than quantitatively measured scores. The reviewed evidence suggests a persistent imbalance between the adoption of marketing innovations and the demonstrated effects on tourism outcomes. User-generated content and electronic word of mouth have the strongest support for their underlying mechanisms among the eight directions examined, whereas influencer marketing, short-form video, social search, generative artificial intelligence, and other rapidly adopted practices are supported by varying levels of empirical evidence. The principal structural challenge concerns attribution: social media platforms effectively measure exposure and engagement, while economically meaningful tourism outcomes often occur at later stages, outside the platform environment, and without reliable data links to the initial exposure. The article approaches marketing innovation as an empirical proposition requiring evaluation rather than merely as an emerging trend to be adopted. It develops an evidence-graded assessment of eight innovative directions, proposes a three-tier strategic adoption framework—adopt now, pilot with measurement, and watch—and identifies a practical visitor-side measurement approach designed to help reduce the attribution gap between social media activities and tourism outcomes.

Saudi mega-projects operate through dense networks of designers, contractors, manufacturers, logistics providers and specialist suppliers, so cost and schedule performance cannot be governed effectively as separate reporting streams. Procurement commitments shape the timing and price of resources; schedule changes alter purchasing priorities and logistics demand; and commercial variations feed back into forecast completion cost. This review develops an integrated framework for cost-schedule and procurement analytics in construction supply chains, with particular relevance to Saudi Arabias Vision 2030 delivery environment. Thirty peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 to 2025 were synthesised across artificial intelligence in construction management, project cost prediction, schedule forecasting, construction supply-chain modelling, resilience and digital-twin-enabled control. The evidence indicates that predictive value emerges when cost, schedule and procurement records share consistent identifiers, timestamps and decision horizons. Machine-learning and hybrid models can improve forecasting, but isolated accuracy is insufficient unless outputs expose uncertainty, identify drivers and trigger accountable management action.

With the rapid development of low-altitude economy (LAE), low-altitude information networks (LAINs) must provide reliable communication, environmental sensing, and target identification to support efficient and safe airspace operation. Although integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) provides a foundation for the joint design of communication and sensing, identification must also be incorporated to meet airspace safety and regulatory requirements. This paper reviews integrated sensing, communications, and identification (ISCAI) for LAE. We first review low-altitude communication, sensing, and identification approaches and explain how representative applications motivate their integration. We then summarize low-altitude ISAC fundamentals, including system architectures, channel modeling, unified signal models, and performance metrics, followed by communication-centric and sensing-centric designs, resource allocation, and aircraft trajectory optimization. Building on these, we introduce ISCAI, focusing on a backscatter communication (BackCom)-based identification mechanism in which backscatter devices serve as electronic license plates for aircraft. We present system and signal models for integrated sensing and identification (ISAI) and ISCAI, together with multifunctional receiver designs and mutual integration gains. Finally, we discuss open problems and future directions, including an information-theoretic framework, artificial intelligence-empowered system design, and reconfigurable intelligent surface-enhanced ISCAI. This review provides a structured perspective on the evolution of LAINs toward integrated communication, sensing, and identification.

BACKGROUND: Precision dosing integrates patient-specific factors to optimize pharmacotherapy. However, current evidence often relies on limited single-center studies, restricting generalizability. METHODS: A narrative review of literature on real-world evidence, pharmacogenetics, biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI), and privacy-preserving data strategies relevant to precision dosing was conducted. RESULTS: Single-center data are insufficient for robust precision-dosing evidence because of small subgroups and local practice biases. Multicenter privacy-preserving systems enable richer, more generalizable datasets that link doses, exposures, genotypes, biomarkers, and outcomes. However, multicenter collaborations should remain aligned with the intended population and should not imply indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous data. Secure pooled environments, federated learning, and synthetic data play distinct method-dependent roles. AI supports exposure estimation, phenotype extraction, and modeling of complex relationships but requires rigorous validation against conventional methods. Causal inference requires epidemiological rigor beyond predictive performance. CONCLUSIONS: Advancing precision dosing requires multicenter, purpose-specific, privacy-preserving, methodologically rigorous, and clinically validated data systems guided by clinical pharmacologists, with AI serving as a complementary tool rather than a default solution.

documents.abstract: College students increasingly use generative AI, yet formal undergraduate classroom implementation remains limited. This study evaluated a structured generative AI training in an undergraduate research methods course, examining its impact on students’ perceptions, self-rated competency, and future intention to use. Early in the semester, students received a lecture on generative AI tools, applications, and ethical issues, including bias, plagiarism, and data privacy. Two optional assignments provided hands-on practice using AI for literature searching and academic writing. After the course, 24 of 195 enrolled students completed a survey. Respondents reported low-to-moderate initial AI familiarity and competency. The lecture was well received and led to confidence in citing and disclosing AI use. Students expressed moderately positive intentions to use AI for future studying and research activities, while reporting concerns about accuracy and academic integrity. Findings suggest that structured, evidence-based AI training may support responsible use in undergraduates while addressing persistent ethical and practical concerns.

documents.abstract: Professional spaces today are rapidly changing, and to meet such swift changes in the environment, there is a rising demand for professionals who understand the dynamics of the place. They need human resources with the competence to perceive, interpret and respond effectively to the influx of their landscapes. Situational Awareness is a skill recognised in aviation, healthcare and domains that require quick responses to changing trajectories. However, it has not received significant attention in higher education despite its potential to develop professional competence and readiness. This article, thereby, aims to investigate the present gap in higher education curricula. It seeks to highlight understanding of situational awareness among the participants in the study, their perception of its need for professional success and the need to integrate it into higher education curricula. It emphasises the role of Situational Awareness in professional development and growth of an individual. The article endeavours to reason its crucial function in the learning phase of a student pursuing Higher Education and also aspires to rationalise its suitability as an important topic of perusal in the curriculum of Higher Education. It explores the vitality of the term and how it helps an individual fit in better in an environment. Personal interaction with the students helped us to analyse their understanding of the concept. In addition, a quantitative and cross-sectional survey design was undertaken for the present research. Data collection was based on structured online questionnaire in the format of six five-point Likert-scale items and demographic questions. The questionnaire incorporated aspects to measure participant's awareness of the term, its professional relevance, appropriate training of situational awareness in higher education, its contribution to boosting employability, whether it improves decision-making and the need for integration into higher education curricula. A sample of 72 participants, including undergraduates, postgraduate students, students with work experience and working professionals from engineering discipline with major emphasis, was used for the study. Descriptive and statistical techniques were deployed for the analysis of the data, particularly the aggregate percentage was taken for the scales reflecting agree and strongly agree parameters which was apparently higher than the neutral, disagree and strongly disagree parameters. The article relies on empirical evidence to assess participants’ perception of situational awareness as a vital skill in the present era. The results aim to inform the value and significance of situational awareness in developing professional competency for stakeholders, that is, curriculum developers, policymakers and higher education entities. The research aspires to contribute to repertoire of competence-based education by investigating as an important transferable skill to hone perception, adaptability and decision making of the students.

This article analyzes the possibilities and limits of Artificial Intelligence in organizing pedagogical evidence aimed at monitoring the learning pathways of students who are the target audience of Special Education. It develops a bibliographic and theoretical-conceptual study grounded in research on Artificial Intelligence and education, pedagogical documentation, mediating assessment, and Inclusive Special Education. It argues that Artificial Intelligence can contribute to systematizing records, integrating different sources of information, and expanding institutional pedagogical memory, but it cannot replace the ethical, relational, and interpretive processes carried out by teachers and pedagogical coordinators. The analysis indicates that data become evidence only when contextualized and interpreted in light of school experiences. It concludes that the contribution of Artificial Intelligence to democratic and inclusive education depends on its articulation with pedagogical documentation and human decisions committed to students’ singularities and to ensuring the right to learn.

ABSTRACT Dynamic graph‐level embedding aims to learn whole‐graph representations from temporal snapshots. Existing methods predominantly follow a single‐vector paradigm that encodes each snapshot as a continuous latent vector, suffering from two key limitations: (1) Stage–Snapshot Entanglement, where within‐stage fluctuations and cross‐stage transitions are conflated without explicit granularity distinction; and (2) Implicit Structural Semantics, where meaningful structural properties remain buried in latent coordinates and are never exposed as interpretable, language‐compatible units. To address these issues, we propose DyGLLM, an LLM‐compatible framework that constructs and aligns dual‐granularity structural representations for dynamic graph understanding. Specifically, DyGLLM maps temporally coherent evolution regimes into selective structural tokens , providing explicit stage‐level anchors in the LLM token space. It further constructs graph fingerprints to verbalize each snapshot's prototype deviation, temporal variation and topological profile into language‐readable structural descriptions. A hybrid structure QA alignment mechanism with LoRA fine‐tuning is then introduced to align structural tokens and graph fingerprints with the LLM's representation space, enabling the model to interpret and reason over explicit structural contexts. Extensive experiments on five dynamic graph benchmarks demonstrate that DyGLLM achieves consistently competitive performance across graph similarity ranking, temporal anomaly detection and change point detection, validating the effectiveness of the proposed dual‐granularity structural representation.

This paper presents InterviewAI, a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform that conducts live mock interviews using artificial intelligence. Candidates often lack access to affordable and realistic interview practice, and existing systems either rely on static question banks or cover only parts of the interview experience. In InterviewAI, a user signs in with Google Authentication and uploads a resume in PDF format. The system extracts skills, education and experience, generates personalised questions, conducts the interview through real-time voice and video conversation with an AI interviewer, and produces a performance report covering strengths, weaknesses, communication skills and suggestions for improvement. A credit-based usage model with Razorpay payment integration makes the platform suitable for production use. The system is built on React.js, Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with Firebase authentication, Razorpay payments and OpenRouter for AI model access, and is deployed on Render. The platform was tried end to end with a few users to check its working, and all core modules, from sign-in to feedback report and payment, worked as intended.

This introduction frames the book as both a personal reflection and a timely response to a rapidly changing world. Rooted in lived experience, it traces how the author’s journey through leadership, crisis, family life, entrepreneurship and inner development deepened the original framework of vocating beyond theory into practice. It also situates the book within a broader trilogy on leadership, business and capital as forces for good, with this edition focusing on how organisations can align purpose with structure, strategy and impact. A central new dimension is the recognition that artificial intelligence is reshaping not only work and learning, but also human identity, contribution and meaning. In response, the Introduction argues that vocation must be made more accessible and adaptive, especially for younger generations whose ways of engaging with knowledge are increasingly digital, interactive and fragmented. This conviction has led to the creation of Vocating.ai, a new venture designed to translate the Seven-Step Framework into a living, technology-enabled platform. The second book is therefore presented not simply as an update, but as a bridge between analogue wisdom and digital possibility in the enduring human search for purpose.

This research examined how road and bus stop design and characteristics influence pedestrian safety, shaping both user perceptions and behaviors, and affecting crash outcomes near transit stops. A three-stage methodology integrated quantitative analysis with empirical field research. The first stage involved a macro-level quantitative analysis of factors contributing to pedestrian crashes, fusing together data on historical crash records, transit operations, demographic data, road inventories, and vehicle counts, and capturing over 300 crash-relevant features. Traditional and machine learning models were applied to classify bus stops and predict crash occurrence and severity. The second stage focused on human factors through a micro-level qualitative investigation, collecting public perceptions of safety through electronic surveys and comparing them with objective risk measures. The third stage consisted of systematic field observations documenting pedestrian behaviors and assessing how environmental and design characteristics influence these behaviors. By integrating objective crash modeling, subjective user perceptions, and observed behavior, the study developed a comprehensive framework for enhancing pedestrian safety. The findings inform actionable design guidelines and policy recommendations, supporting Vision Zero objectives and guiding transit agency standards, municipal complete streets policies, and national street design manuals.

An AI administrator walks into an Honors English seminar. The assignment: prepare undergraduates to help write the course AI policy. This UNLV case study follows an unusual collaboration between a professor of postcolonial literature and the administrator of the university’s ChatGPT and Claude environments. The administrator also wrote UNLV’s draft institutional AI framework and experiences classroom AI rules as a PhD student. The session asks what becomes possible when the person who sees the systems behind the interface joins faculty and students in the policy conversation. Before students could write the rules, they needed enough technical literacy to understand what they were governing: model limitations, learning tradeoffs, differences between consumer and institutional accounts, data practices, authorship, transparency, and personal boundaries. The presenters will trace how that foundation prepared students to participate in course policy development. Dr. Beth Rosenberg will share why she invited IT into an English seminar, how students responded, and how the policy took shape. Attendees will leave with an adaptable model for combining IT knowledge, faculty expertise, and student agency to create AI expectations grounded in both technology and learning.

In the 2021 Census, 5.8 million people in Australia (22.8%) used a language other than English at home, and 872,000 said they spoke English not well or not at all. For people from refugee and migrant backgrounds, the first barrier to mental health care is often simply being understood. Services report that many clinicians do not engage interpreters, and when a consultation does cross languages, the patient's own words, idioms and explanations of distress are easily lost between the interpreter, the clinician and the record. Victoria's Royal Commission into its mental health system recommended developing digital technologies to deliver language services. This paper reports the design of Aperta Health, a web-based prototype that uses generative AI to help clinicians and bicultural workers turn multilingual or interpreter-mediated accounts into a structured, safety-conscious clinical record without discarding the original words. Its core design move is a strict division of labour. Deterministic code scores screening instruments and applies coded crisis rules. Generative AI only extracts, translates and drafts within bounded formats, and is told to write "Not stated in narrative" rather than invent findings. Qualified professionals interpret, diagnose, prescribe and escalate. We describe the design principles and architecture, then assess the prototype against Australian regulation. We conclude that several functions, including AI-drafted diagnostic formulations and public self-assessment, would be unlikely to qualify for the Therapeutic Goods Administration's exemption for clinical decision support software, and that the prototype's data flows do not yet meet the privacy expectations set out in national clinical AI guidance. We state these limits plainly. The prototype runs only on synthetic data, has not been clinically evaluated, and is not supplied for clinical use. The contribution is a reusable design pattern for language-inclusive mental health documentation, and an honest map of what stands between such a prototype and safe use. documents.abstract: Data analytics is changing how organisations operate, plan, and compete. Businesses use data to understand customer behaviour, improve services, reduce costs, and identify new opportunities. As digital systems expand, companies collect information from websites, applications, transactions, supply chains, and customer interactions. They need skilled professionals who can turn this information into clear and useful insights. At the same time, the field is evolving. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, cloud analytics, real-time reporting, and automated data preparation are changing how analysts work. These developments are creating new opportunities, but they also require learners to build strong foundations and keep their skills current. Choosing a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet requires more than checking a course title. Learners should understand the current trends in the industry, the tools employers use, and the skills required for different career paths. This knowledge can help them select relevant training and prepare for the changing demands of the data analytics profession. The Growing Importance of Data Analytics Organisations no longer use data only to prepare monthly reports. They use it to support decisions across sales, finance, marketing, operations, healthcare, manufacturing, and technology. For example, a retailer can analyse sales records to forecast product demand. A bank can study transaction patterns to identify suspicious activity. A hospital can use operational reports to plan staff and resources. A marketing team can measure campaign performance to understand which activities produce results. These applications depend on accurate data, suitable analytical methods, and clear communication. Analysts must understand the business problem before selecting tools or drawing conclusions. The market outlook also reflects the growing role of analytics. Grand View Research estimated that India's data analytics market generated approximately US$4.23 billion in revenue in 2025 and projected that it could reach around US$47.51 billion by 2033. The forecast represents an estimated compound annual growth rate of 36.1% from 2026 to 2033. These are market projections, not guaranteed employment or salary outcomes. For learners considering a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet, this growth highlights the value of developing practical skills that can be applied across industries. Artificial Intelligence and AI-Assisted Analytics Artificial intelligence is one of the most important trends in the analytics industry. AI tools can help analysts summarise datasets, identify patterns, generate queries, and automate routine tasks. This can reduce the time spent on some activities and allow professionals to focus more on interpreting results. For example, an analyst can use AI-assisted tools to explore sales performance or generate an initial summary of customer feedback. The analyst must still verify the output, check the data, and confirm that the conclusions are valid. In June 2026, Gartner identified AI-first operations, AI governance, and connected data and analytics platforms among the major trends shaping enterprise analytics. Its report also highlighted the need to manage the risks associated with AI-driven decisions. Learners should therefore understand both the benefits and the limits of AI. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet can provide a foundation in data analysis, while further learning can help students explore AI-assisted workflows. Important areas to understand include: Using AI tools to support data exploration. Checking AI-generated calculations and summaries. Understanding the basics of machine learning. Protecting confidential information when using AI systems. Applying human judgement to important business decisions. AI can support analytical work, but it does not remove the need for accurate data, sound reasoning, and accountability. Predictive and Prescriptive Analytics Traditional reporting often explains what has already happened. Predictive and prescriptive analytics extend this process by helping organisations estimate possible outcomes and assess potential actions. Predictive Analytics Predictive analytics uses historical data, statistical methods, and machine learning models to estimate future events. A retailer may forecast product demand from previous sales. A financial institution may estimate credit risk. A logistics company may use historical delivery information to identify the factors linked to delays. Learners should understand basic statistics, data preparation, and model evaluation before moving into advanced predictive techniques. Python and SQL can also support this work. Prescriptive Analytics Prescriptive analytics goes a step further by assessing possible actions based on defined objectives and constraints. For example, a supply chain team may use an optimisation model to assess delivery routes or inventory levels. Grand View Research identified predictive analytics as the largest segment of India's data analytics market by revenue in 2025, while its forecast identified prescriptive analytics as the fastest-growing type segment over the projection period. These developments show the value of understanding analytical methods beyond basic reporting. Learners considering a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should review whether the syllabus covers statistical reasoning and introduces advanced analytics at an appropriate level. Real-Time Data Analytics and Streaming Businesses increasingly need information as events occur. Real-time analytics helps teams monitor new data and respond to changes without waiting for a monthly or weekly report. For example, an e-commerce company can track order activity and inventory levels during a major sale. A transport company can monitor vehicle performance and delivery status. A financial organisation can use real-time systems to flag transactions that require further review. Real-time analytics often depends on data pipelines, cloud infrastructure, streaming technologies, and reliable monitoring systems. Entry-level analysts may not build these systems themselves, but an understanding of how data moves from source to dashboard can help them work more effectively with technical teams. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should ideally teach learners the fundamentals of data collection, cleaning, and reporting before introducing more advanced real-time applications. Cloud Analytics and Modern Data Platforms Cloud analytics allows organisations to store, process, and analyse data through cloud-based services. It can help teams access information across locations and connect datasets from different business systems. Cloud platforms also support collaboration and scalable data processing. However, effective cloud analytics requires suitable access controls, cost management, data quality checks, and security practices. Modern data platforms increasingly bring together data engineering, analytics, governance, and AI capabilities. This creates a need for professionals who understand not only how to create a report but also where the data comes from and how it should be used. For beginners, the practical starting point is to understand spreadsheets, databases, SQL, data models, and visualisation tools. After building this foundation, learners can explore cloud data services and more advanced analytical workflows. Business Intelligence and Data Visualisation Business intelligence remains a key part of modern analytics. Organisations need clear dashboards and reports that help teams monitor performance and act on relevant findings. Tools such as Microsoft Power BI and Tableau help users present information through charts, tables, filters, and interactive dashboards. Excel remains useful for organising data and performing basic analysis. A well-designed dashboard can show revenue trends, customer retention, inventory levels, and operating costs in one place. The analyst must choose suitable metrics and explain their meaning without creating misleading impressions. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet that includes practical reporting exercises can help learners understand these concepts. When reviewing a programme, check whether it covers data preparation, dashboard design, data modelling, and the interpretation of business metrics. Data Quality, Privacy, and Responsible Analytics Advanced tools cannot compensate for poor-quality data. Missing values, duplicate records, incorrect formats, and inconsistent definitions can lead to inaccurate reports. Data quality and governance have become even more important as organisations expand their use of AI and self-service analytics. TechTarget's January 2026 review of business intelligence trends highlighted governance, data quality, and responsible access to analytics as important concerns for organisations. Learners should develop habits that support reliable analysis: Check the source and completeness of a dataset. Identify duplicate records and inconsistent values. Confirm that calculations use the correct definitions. Protect personal and confidential information. Document assumptions and limitations. Avoid drawing conclusions that the data cannot support. These practices apply to every industry. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should help learners recognise that responsible data handling is part of professional analytics, not an optional extra. The Rise of Self-Service Analytics Self-service analytics allows business users to explore approved datasets and create reports with less dependence on specialist teams. documents.abstract: Abstract Radiological reports, which document radiologists’ imaging observations and diagnostic conclusions from CT, X-ray and MRI scans, deliver core imaging evidence for clinical diagnosis and therapeutic planning. Inaccurate or disordered reports may lead to misdiagnosis and delayed intervention, posing risks to patient safety. Radiological reports are essential for clinical decision-making, yet Chinese radiology reports frequently exhibit logical inconsistencies, incomplete content, non-standardized descriptions, and formatting errors, while manual quality control remains time-consuming and inconsistent. Large teacher models can provide task-specific supervision but are difficult to deploy locally, whereas smaller models require adaptation to this clinical text task. We developed a teacher-supervised, locally deployable 4B language-model system for rule-based textual quality control of Chinese radiology reports.Among the three evaluated teacher APIs, Doubao-seed1.6-non-thinking achieved the highest macro-precision ,0.94, under the study's precision-prioritized selection.Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 emerged as the optimal student model, achieving an average precision of 0.90, recall of 0.49, and F1 score of 0.62, with inference speed improved by over 40-fold. Real-world clinical validation demonstrated that the lightweight model attains a precision of 0.74 in authentic clinical scenarios while retaining high overall performance, satisfying the deployment demands of on-site clinical institutions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: KV cache reuse is one of the most effective ways to reduce LLM inference cost, but today its benefits are largely confined to a single cluster. When a provider serves the same model across geographically distributed regions, each region may repeatedly prefill the same popular prefixes, wasting GPU time and increasing time-to-first-token (TTFT). Exploiting reuse across regions involves discovering which worker currently holds a reusable KV cache for each request's prefix. We show that this KV cache discovery problem is structurally harder than conventional object lookup. Unlike hash-placement mechanisms such as DHTs, where an object's location is a deterministic function of its key, KV caches are created on the workers that serve requests, and their holder sets change with subsequent requests and KV cache evictions. KV cache discovery therefore calls for decoupling KV cache identity from placement. We present KVCompass, a discovery plane for Internet-scale KV cache sharing. The discovery index supports variable-length prefix lookup with constant-time local table reads at the edge, allowing each request to be forwarded to the worker that best balances KV cache reuse against load and network distance. Evaluation includes a 64-worker geo-distributed simulation and a 14-worker three-continent real-machine testbed. Evaluation shows that KVCompass achieves $1.3-14\times$ lower P99 TTFT than the baselines, up to $3.7\times$ lower P99 end-to-end latency, up to $4.7\times$ the throughput, and a peak load factor within 2% of the Oracle floor.

This review article examines how three key variables of contemporary educational reform come together: curricular mainstreaming, competency-based learning, and student-centeredness. Drawing on a qualitative, descriptive and documentary methodology based on the systematization of twenty relevant studies published between 2024 and 2026, it analyzes the behavior, evolution and operational tensions among these pedagogical trends. The results show that mainstreaming works as the methodological scaffold that unsettles fragmented traditional knowledge and enables the mobilization of complex competencies in the classroom. They also confirm that student-centered approaches meaningfully increase intrinsic motivation, socio-environmental awareness and critical thinking skills. The study reviews operational limitations as well, including teacher resistance and the administrative complexity involved in designing integrated curricula. It concludes that the convergence of these three dimensions is not a decorative addition to didactic planning but a necessary condition for building a deep, ethical education with a strong sense of civic responsibility amid the dynamics of the knowledge society.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

Large-scale diffusion models are commonly trained with a constant learning rate (LR) and exponential moving average (EMA), despite the strong performance of LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization in training large language models. We study whether EMA is uniquely suited to diffusion training, or whether stronger alternatives have been underexplored. Our theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limitation, whereas LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization admit vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions. Empirically, LR decay and EMA provide complementary benefits: combining decay with EMA further improves the standard baseline at most tested starting points, although the gain remains sensitive to when decay begins. Schedule-Free avoids this timing requirement and consistently outperforms EMA with a constant LR across training stages, achieving both lower fixed-evaluation objectives and better generation quality. Our analysis further shows that all three strategies substantially reduce parameter variability, yet stronger stabilization is not always better: EMA with a constant LR retains comparatively higher parameter variability, while aggressive decay combined with EMA achieves the lowest checkpoint variability but also weakens continued optimization. Schedule-Free substantially reduces parameter variability while preserving more late-stage progress, providing a better balance between parameter stability and continued optimization. Finally, the benefits of Schedule-Free extend beyond pretraining to ReFL and generator-side DMD, demonstrating its transferability across distinct diffusion optimization settings. Overall, our results suggest that large diffusion models need more than parameter averaging alone: effective optimization requires balancing variance reduction with continued optimization.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objectives To evaluate whether large language model assistance improves radiologists’ agreement with a text-based reference standard in inferring the modified American Heart Association carotid plaque classification from free-text MRI reports, and whether a lightweight model can perform well under criteria-guided prompting. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 433 patients from three institutions. In a report-based reader study, four radiologists classified MRI reports with and without large language model assistance. In standalone evaluation, a rule-based baseline and 10 models were compared under naive and criteria-guided prompting. The reference standard was expert consensus based on the report text. Results Among 433 patients (mean age, 65.9 years ± 13.4; 248 males), AI assistance improved six-class agreement with the text-based reference standard. At the vessel level, junior radiologists improved from 61.75% to 83.12% (Qwen3-8B) and 87.75% (DeepSeek-R1); senior radiologists from 77.00% to 87.50% and 92.25%, respectively (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001). Patient-level agreement increased from 41.0% to 78.8% (junior) and from 59.8% to 87.8% (senior) with DeepSeek-R1. Agreement increased (quadratic-weighted κ : 0.231 without AI vs 0.775 with DeepSeek-R1). In standalone evaluation, criteria-guided prompting improved Qwen3-8B agreement from 38.91% to 81.52% (95% CI: 78.87–84.06%), remaining 5.89 percentage points below DeepSeek-R1 (87.41%; 95% CI: 85.10–89.61%). Conclusion In this report-based classification setting, large language model assistance improved radiologists’ agreement with the text-based reference standard, with larger gains in junior radiologists. When prompts explicitly encoded AHA criteria, an 8B local candidate model performed well, supporting its potential use as a standardization aid for text-based workflows. Key Points Question Report-based modified AHA classification of carotid plaques is experience-dependent and difficult to standardize, as mapping multi-sequence imaging findings to classification conclusions imposes substantial cognitive load. Findings Large language model assistance improved agreement with a text-based reference standard and raised inter-reader consistency (weighted κ 0.231–0.775), narrowing the junior–senior gap. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91–81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

documents.abstract: Purpose: To describe laryngeal disorders among open-air market vendors and identify the most prevalent disorders, lesion types, affected laryngeal regions, and associated risk factors.Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted involving 49 open-air market vendors from Aracaju, Northeastern Brazil.Participants underwent structured interviews and videonasolaryngoscopic examination.Demographic, occupational, clinical, and laryngeal findings were analyzed descriptively.Results: Women represented 63.3% of participants.Hoarseness was reported by 55% of the sample.Symptoms suggestive of laryngopharyngeal reflux were highly prevalent.Videolaryngoscopy revealed abnormalities in all laryngeal compartments, with the highest prevalence occurring in the posterior laryngeal and subglottic regions.Interarytenoid and retrocricoid edema and hyperemia, with or without pachydermia, were the predominant findings.Vocal fold cysts predominated among women, whereas vocal fold thickening and polyps were more common among men.Conclusion: Open-air market vendors should be considered a distinct category of professional voice users.Laryngopharyngeal reflux was the most prevalent disorder and the posterior laryngeal/subglottic region was the most frequently affected site.Preventive occupational health measures focusing on vocal hygiene and reflux control are warranted.

Background Work readiness refers to the comprehensive competencies required for individuals to enter and adapt to the workforce. It is relevant to the transition from nursing student to clinical nurse. However, existing research has paid limited attention to heterogeneity in nursing interns’ work readiness, and few studies have examined associated factors from the perspective of Social Cognitive Career Theory. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of work readiness among nursing interns and examine the associations of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) literacy and the clinical learning environment with profile membership. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 712 final-year nursing interns from three nursing schools in Anhui Province, China, between November 2025 and June 2026. Participants completed the Nursing Practice Readiness Scale, Clinical Learning Environment Questionnaire, and Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Latent Profile Analysis was used to identify distinct work readiness profiles, and multinomial logistic regression was performed to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results Three latent profiles of work readiness were identified: low work readiness ( n = 415, 58.3%), moderate work readiness ( n = 227, 31.9%), and high work readiness ( n = 70, 9.8%). The overall multinomial logistic regression model( χ 2 = 467.253, P < 0.001) showed that the clinical learning environment, GenAI literacy, academic performance, clinical learning outcomes, and sense of professional belonging were significantly associated with work readiness profile membership (all P < 0.05). Conclusions Three distinct work readiness profiles were identified among nursing interns. Clinical learning environment, GenAI literacy, academic performance, clinical learning outcomes, and sense of professional belonging were associated with profile membership. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of nursing interns’ work readiness and may inform the development of individualized educational support strategies.

Generative AI will shape health care less through model fluency alone than through the workforce and institutions prepared to use it responsibly. Anchored in UCLA Health’s randomized trial of ambient AI scribes, this chapter treats generative AI as workforce infrastructure: a socio-technical arrangement involving models, interfaces, consent, training, review, supervision, and local support. Evidence from ambient documentation, AI-assisted inbox replies, patient messaging, and UC Health’s developing memory-care redesign shows that generative AI does not eliminate professional responsibility; it redistributes work from first-draft production toward verification, exception handling, relational communication, supervision, and workflow redesign. Placed within the book’s five transformations, these tools can accelerate capture, synthesis, and drafting, but cannot replace standards, governance, or accountable enactment. The chapter identifies hallucination, omission, overconfidence, hidden correction burden, uneven adoption, privacy, and changing local conditions as limits requiring continuous stewardship. It then defines the next-generation workforce through integrated capabilities in AI and data literacy, critical appraisal, escalation judgment, human factors, patient communication, interdisciplinary collaboration, change management, and bioequity monitoring. Education must therefore move beyond prompting to supervised practice and accountable review. The chapter concludes that future readiness requires portfolio visibility, role-specific training, explicit review and escalation standards, patient transparency, postdeployment monitoring, redesign capacity, and leadership able to preserve trust while governing continuous adaptation.

Executive Overview This document presents an independent institutional infrastructure proposal titled “Lecture Theatre Rehabilitation and Classroom Seating Capacity Expansion Project," developed as a turnkey capital intervention model for Kaduna Polytechnic, Kaduna State, Nigeria. Designed to eliminate severe classroom congestion and safety hazards resulting from shortages of functional furniture, this proposal establishes a comprehensive framework for modernizing lecture halls, refurbishing civil structures, and deploying heavy-duty, ergonomic student seating across central academic complexes. Technical Scope & Infrastructure Pillars The proposed intervention covers four primary spatial and structural pillars: 1. Civil & Architectural Refurbishment: Complete floor leveling, acoustic ceiling repairs, wall re-plastering/painting, and lighting restoration across major central lecture halls and auditoriums. 2. Furniture Procurement & Capacity Expansion: Design, local fabrication, and installation of durable, dual-seat metal-frame desk units and fixed auditorium seating to accommodate over 4,000 students simultaneously. 3. Safety & Universal Design Compliance: Re-configuration of seating layouts to adhere to international emergency egress standards, wider gangways, and dedicated accessible seating areas for students with mobility impairments. 4. Maintenance & Asset Tracking System: Implementation of institutional asset-tagging and a preventative maintenance schedule to protect public physical infrastructure from rapid wear and degradation. Financial Framework & Project Metrics · Proposed Beneficiary Institution: Kaduna Polytechnic, Kaduna State, Nigeria · Target Supervising Units: Directorate of Works and Physical Planning & School Deans / Academic Board · Implementation Duration: 6 Months · Total Estimated Budget: ₦107,697,500 NGN (Approx. $81,000 USD at interbank rates) · Target Funding Mechanism: OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID) – Public Sector Operations Grant / Loan Facility. Purpose & Open-Access Availability This document is published on Zenodo as an open-access policy and educational facilities engineering model. It serves as an actionable benchmark for university administrators, social infrastructure planners, educational policy researchers, and multilateral funding agencies seeking structured templates for classroom capacity expansion in developing economies.

Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, enabling non-autoregressive text generation through parallel decoding. Existing dLLMs can be broadly categorized into two families: masked diffusion models (MDMs) and uniform diffusion models (UDMs) In this work, we theoretically show that MDMs are easier to optimize due to their mask-based transition schedule but have lower computational expressivity, whereas UDMs enable iterative state revision and greater expressivity but are substantially harder to train. This trade-off raises a natural question: can we obtain the expressivity of iterative revision without giving up the simple, easy-to-optimize transition schedule of MDMs? Motivated by this analysis, we propose Lookahead Editing (\ours{}), which augments masked diffusion decoding with a rewritable proposal state. At each decoding step, the model performs several lookahead updates to iteratively refine future predictions in this proposal state before committing tokens to the masked sequence. This design introduces a rewritable proposal that uses additional compute to improve expressivity while keeping the simple mask-based transition schedule of MDMs. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B to obtain LED-\texttt{7B} and LED-\texttt{8B}, respectively. Across eight benchmarks, LED SFT yields average gains of $+11.4$ and $+7.7$ points over standard MDM SFT. Moreover, using SFT alone, LED-\texttt{8B} outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B Q-mode, which is trained with continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.

documents.abstract: The article examines India’s 2026 amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules in relation to synthetically generated information, covering deepfake creation and distribution. It first identifies the need for regulation in India, drawing on recent instances of deepfake-related events, and then places those needs in a comparative perspective by analysing regulatory approaches in China, the European Union and the United States. The article argues that India has adopted a hybrid intermediary-liability model that combines labelling, provenance, technical-prevention, user-declaration and accelerated takedown obligations while still relying on existing criminal, electoral, consumer-protection, privacy and personality-rights frameworks to do much of the hard work. By situating India’s framework within the broader global regulatory environment, the article contributes to current debates on how legal systems should respond to harmful synthetic media without unduly constraining other beneficial uses of generative AI. Overall, the analysis shows that India’s Intermediary Guidelines Amendments offer a reasonable response to the main issues at stake but leave considerable room for other areas of law to do the heavy lifting. The article concludes on a cautionary note, highlighting the expected challenges of future implementation.

We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the optimization of their compilation.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have greatly assisted legal professionals. However, our empirical studies reveal that, when faced with underspecified consultations from non-experts, current LLMs often produce irresponsible responses with limited utility despite lacking sufficient case details for definitive conclusions. To better assist laypeople, legal LLMs must identify focal points of dispute and proactively elicit crucial context from users. Unfortunately, existing data resources often focus on interaction and response quality, offering limited insight into how proactive interaction affects LLMs' downstream claim-level judgment prediction in actual civil cases. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{LexPilot}, a benchmark linking proactive legal interaction to claim-level verdict prediction using authentic Chinese civil judgments. Constructed from 432 real-world judgments across 36 common causes of action, LexPilot comprises expert-reviewed pairs of complete and underspecified consultation histories with corresponding court verdicts. Experiments reveal that current LLMs struggle with proactive legal interactions in underspecified consultations, with downstream judgment prediction substantially underperforming that in the fully specified consultation setup (-23.84% on average). Further analysis identifies critical bottlenecks hindering these capabilities. Our work highlights the urgent need for more user-centered legal AI to better serve the public.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed through systems in which authority, execution, oversight, and consequence no longer belong to the same actor. A model may be developed by one organization, integrated by another, configured by an enterprise, instructed by a human, executed through an AI agent, routed through external tools, and experienced by a person who had no role in any of those decisions. The resulting liability problem is not adequately described by asking whether a human remained "in the loop" or whether an audit trail exists. This working paper develops the GAILC Authority Boundary framework. It defines the Authority Boundary as the point at which consequential decision rights, discretion, intervention responsibility, or consequence-bearing responsibility passes from one actor, system, organization, or layer to another, and analyses each boundary through five elements: Authority, Transfer, Reliance, Intervention, and Consequence. The framework identifies two difficult liability cases that conventional control models often leave unresolved. Intended-Execution Liability concerns harm produced when a system remains within its authority, follows policy, uses permitted tools, and operates substantially as designed. No-Action Liability concerns harm produced or worsened where an actor bears an identifiable duty or assigned responsibility to act, possesses the authority, information, timing, and practical capacity to do so, yet no consequential intervention occurs. The paper introduces the Authority Envelope, the distinction between authorization and judgment, the Silence-as-Authority Problem, the GAILC Allocation Test, Consequence Ownership, Allocation Completeness and Allocation Adequacy, Residual Consequence, and Orphaned Harm. It proposes a standardized Authority Boundary Record (ABR) designed to support verification, contestability, and independent adjudication, together with a boundary failure taxonomy, an irreversibility threshold, an inter-organizational allocation procedure, and a pre-deployment test. Its central proposition is that traceability is evidence, not allocation: an authority and execution chain may be fully reconstructable while accountability and consequence allocation remain incomplete. The framework is analytical and does not determine legal liability. It is positioned in relation to agency law, duties concerning failures to act, design-defect analysis, and scholarship on the problem of many hands, responsibility gaps, and moral crumple zones. This paper is the third in the GAILC Working Paper series, following WP001 (The Human Presence Economy) and WP002 (The Intervention Test).

documents.abstract: Abstract Welding efficiency and environmental performance are critical in industrial applications. This study presents a cradle to gate life cycle assessment (LCA) comparing conventional tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding with activated tungsten inert gas (A-TIG) welding for producing 100 mm bead-on-plate welds on grade 304L stainless steel. In A TIG, a TiO₂ methanol flux allows a lower welding current while achieving a comparable penetration depth. Calculated welding electricity consumption, measured flux-preparation electricity consumption, and material inputs were modeled in SimaPro 9.2 using Ecoinvent 3 datasets. Midpoint impacts were assessed using the EPD 2018 method, and endpoint impacts were assessed using ReCiPe 2016 Hierarchist method. Results show that A-TIG reduced welding electricity consumption by approximately 40% compared with TIG and yielded lower modeled acidification, eutrophication, and global warming potentials. Water scarcity impacts were nearly identical for the two processes. However, However, A-TIG’s normalized photochemical ozone creation potential (POCP) score was 68.1 percentage points higher than TIG’s, with the higher impact set to 100% in each category, primarily because of modeled methanol emissions and upstream flux-production impacts. A one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis covering 30 scenarios showed that the comparative ranking of the two processes remained unchanged within the investigated parameter ranges, with methanol mass identified as the dominant influence on POCP. Endpoint modeling indicated that the human-health category dominated the weighted damage profile. These results represent potential life-cycle impacts rather than measured occupational health effects. This experimental cradle-to-gate LCA of penetration-matched bead-on-plate welding indicates that flux-assisted welding can reduce several impacts associated with electricity consumption while introducing trade-offs related to photochemical ozone creation. These findings support the optimization of activating flux formulations and welding parameters within the investigated conditions, while their applicability to industrial joints requires further validation.

General Background The pre-analytical stage represents a critical phase within clinical laboratory testing sequences because it involves initial procedures largely reliant on manual handling and personnel precision. Specific Background Implementation of Internal Quality Improvement (IQI) serves as the primary evaluation tool to analyze pre-analytical factors affecting clinical laboratory test results. Knowledge Gap Although overall pre-analytical quality appears optimal, recurring human-factor errors during critical operational points remain inadequately mitigated across routine workflows. Aims This study evaluates pre-analytical variables influencing laboratory test accuracy and assesses the role of educational interventions in mitigating human-induced errors. Results Findings indicate that while internal quality performance generally ranges from good to very good, critical vulnerabilities persist during patient identification, phlebotomy execution, and anticoagulant-to-specimen volume ratios. Novelty This literature review synthesizes multi-year publication data from 2015 to 2015 to map recurrent pre-analytical discrepancies and evaluate targeted educational impacts. Implications Systematic staff education and standardized compliance significantly enhance procedural reliability and clinical diagnostic safety. Key Findings Highlights Pre-analytical error rates are predominantly driven by manual handling vulnerabilities during patient identification and sample collection, Phlebotomy technique discrepancies and sample-to-anticoagulant ratio deviations significantly compromise test result accuracy, Structured educational interventions effectively improve staff compliance and reduce human-factor errors. Keywords Pre-Analytical, Internal Quality Improvement, Clinical Laboratory, Laboratory Errors, Quality Control
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

documents.abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.
